text: The town sets its course: {变量1}.
Farmers want more irrigation channels and clinics. Salvage workers want to explore for ore below the hillside. The craftsmen spread their hands: both sides are short-staffed.
This policy will set the town's research priorities for this phase. Once chosen, it cannot be changed.
The crops are ripening fast, and there aren't enough hands. The farmers have come asking the school to close for two seasons so the teachers can take the older children to help bring in the harvest.
But the teacher presses a hand on the textbook and says that if classes stop now, the children will fall behind for the whole year.
Pause classes to help harvest (assign two teachers to farming)
{分支1} rolled up their trousers and went to the fields. For now, the school will keep only its literacy classes. {分支2}
Shift assignments returned to manual control. Jobs will remain as agreed this time.
The school bell rings as usual. The farmers have no choice but to pack the harvest shifts more tightly.
Black smoke from the smelting furnace hangs over the town all day. People with coughs and wheezing line up at the clinic, and the medical staff come asking for an explanation.
The furnace must keep running to meet the demand for iron ingots. But if one shift takes a break, the children's lungs might get a few days of relief.
Cut one smelting shift (return two smelters to idle)
One shift of workers has been pulled from the smelting furnace.
The clinic has received a new supply of cough and lung medicine.
The furnace burns day and night as usual. Many people quietly take note of the cost.
Several toolmakers have jointly proposed running the tool bench themselves: if they tend the furnace and tools day and night, output could increase by two-tenths.

In return, one quarter of each batch of tools must be kept by the cooperative. When the town's public stores have fewer than 15 tools, the town will buy them back at 1 food per tool. If the public workshop keeps running it, all output goes to the public stores, and production stays at its current pace.
Hand it over to the Toolmakers' Cooperative
The Toolmakers' Cooperative now runs the tool bench. Cooperative stores and public-store buybacks are accounted for separately.
Keep it under the public workshop
The tool bench remains with the public workshop. All tools produced go to the public stores.
The craftswoman who was the first to fall by the furnace can no longer push a plane. She slides her polished toolbox to the center of the table.
“The furnace, the doors and windows, the traps outside. I've kept an eye on them all these years. Now it's time for a steadier pair of hands to take over.”
Hand it to a workshop apprentice (requires a toolmaker on duty)
The apprentice takes the heavy toolbox. As long as a toolmaker is on duty in the workshop, the furnace will still produce 2 extra wood every 10 seconds.
Residents will take turns tending the fire and making routine repairs. They can gather 1 extra wood every 10 seconds.
Complete one joint project with a neighbor
Craftsmen and farmers have drawn up plans for earthen row houses. They require no metal, only wood, tools, and the neighbors' labor.
The cooperative row houses are complete, adding thirty-two beds beneath their roofs. Residents will take turns handling repairs from now on.
